requirements: The core contributions of DiP-SD (Distributed Pipelined Speculative Decoding) have been reproduced, including the joint optimization framework, latency/utility models, and numerical results demonstrating throughput gains over baselines.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware environment, Qwen3 model series, and profiling-based latency parameters have been set up as described in Section IV-A and Table II.
Hardware and software environment for the device-edge deployment has been provisioned to match the paper's setup.

Code/scripts have been implemented that document the draft-side hardware as an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU (used to host the Qwen3-1.7B draft model) via a hardware configuration file or environment probe.
Code/scripts have been implemented that document the edge-server hardware as an NVIDIA A100-80GB GPU (used to host the Qwen3-32B target/verify model).
Code has been implemented that installs and pins the required Python dependencies including PySCIPOpt (with SCIP backend) and a Hugging Face transformers-compatible stack able to load Qwen3 models.
The Qwen3 draft and target models and their transformer dimension constants have been acquired and encoded as used in the paper.
Code has been implemented that downloads/loads the Qwen3-1.7B draft model checkpoint and makes it available for local drafting on the device side.
Code has been implemented that downloads/loads the Qwen3-32B target model checkpoint and makes it available for verification on the server side.
The draft model transformer dimensions (J^d, h_1^d, h_2^d) are set to (28, 2048, 6144) in the configuration used by the optimizer and latency functions.
The verify model transformer dimensions (J^v, h_1^v, h_2^v) are set to (64, 5120, 25600) in the configuration used by the optimizer and latency functions.
Latency parameters have been obtained by profiling each model on its hardware and fitting the affine latency model in equations (5)-(6).

Code has been implemented that profiles per-step draft-model latency on the RTX 3090 across varying context/draft lengths and records latency samples for fitting the affine model t = c * b * F + beta.
Code has been implemented that profiles per-step verify-model latency on the A100-80GB across varying batch sizes and (L, I) values, and records latency samples for fitting the affine model.

Code has been implemented that performs a linear least-squares fit of the affine latency model (per equations (5)-(6)) using the profiled samples to produce (c, beta) coefficients for both draft and verify sides.
The default user-side latency parameters (c_m, beta_m) are configured to (4.0305e-11, 33.8151) as specified in Table II, with c_m in ms per compute unit and beta_m in ms.
The verify-side timing parameters (c^v, beta^v) are configured to (1.2077e-11, 95.1074) as specified in Table II.
Default system parameters (user number, acceptance rate, prefix length, comm latency, initial draft length, memory cap, and bounds) have been configured per Table II.
The default configuration sets user number M=6, scan range of N from 2 to M, default acceptance rate alpha_m=0.78, and default prefix length i_m=512 as specified in Table II.
The default acceptance rate 0.78 has been produced/verified by estimating draft-token acceptance from inference statistics over 100 sampled prompts using the Qwen3-1.7B/Qwen3-32B pair.
The default communication latency tau^c_m=3.0 ms and initial draft length l_m=7 are configured as constants used by the optimizer and simulator.
The edge-server memory cap Gamma^v_max is set to 8.0e10 bytes in the memory feasibility constraint.
The practical variable bounds (L_ub, I_ub, T_ub, S_ub) are set to (20, 1024, 1e6, 3e6) and passed as upper bounds to the MILP subproblems.
Unit conventions are enforced in code: all latency parameters/variables are expressed in milliseconds (ms), memory in bytes (B), and throughput reported as 1000 * U(l)/S in token/s.
The per-user utility function u_m(l_m) and total accepted-tokens function U(l) capturing the geometric acceptance model with bonus token have been implemented as in Section II-B.
The per-user utility function u_m(l_m) implementing the geometric acceptance model with a guaranteed bonus token has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that defines a function u_m(l_m, alpha_m) taking a positive integer draft length l_m and an acceptance rate alpha_m in (0,1), and returns the expected number of accepted tokens in one speculative round for user m.

Code has been implemented so that u_m(l_m, alpha_m) evaluates to (1 - alpha_m^(l_m+1)) / (1 - alpha_m), matching Equation (1) (the closed form of the geometric acceptance model summed over l_m draft tokens plus one bonus token).
Code has been implemented such that u_m(l_m=0, alpha_m) = 1 for any alpha_m in (0,1), reflecting the always-generated bonus token when no draft tokens are proposed.

Code has been implemented such that u_m(l_m, alpha_m) is monotonically non-decreasing in l_m for any fixed alpha_m in (0,1), and asymptotically approaches 1/(1 - alpha_m) as l_m grows (diminishing returns property invoked to justify bounding l_m in Section III-C).
The total accepted-tokens function U(l) aggregating per-user utilities across all M users has been implemented per Equation (2).

Code has been implemented that defines a function U(l, alpha) taking the vector of draft lengths l = (l_1,...,l_M) and per-user acceptance rates alpha = (alpha_1,...,alpha_M) and returns the total expected accepted tokens across all M users.
Code has been implemented such that U(l, alpha) equals sum_{m=1}^{M} u_m(l_m, alpha_m), consistent with Equation (2).

Code has been implemented that vectorizes U(l, alpha) over per-user parameters (supports heterogeneous alpha_m across users) and returns a scalar numerator suitable for use in the throughput objective R = U(l)/S.
A binary-selector lookup form of the utility, u_m^{lookup}(y_m) = sum_{k=1}^{L_ub} y_{m,k} * u_m(k, alpha_m), has been implemented for use inside the l-subproblem MILP as defined by Equation (32).
Code has been implemented that precomputes the lookup table u_m(k, alpha_m) for k in {1,...,L_ub} for each user m, using the geometric acceptance model with bonus token from Equation (1).

Code has been implemented that, given binary selectors y_{m,k} satisfying sum_k y_{m,k} = 1, returns u_m^{lookup} = sum_k y_{m,k} * u_m(k, alpha_m) and, together with l_m = sum_k k * y_{m,k}, reproduces the value of u_m(l_m) for the selected integer draft length.
The compute-intensity functions F^d, F^v and the affine per-step latency functions G_m and G^v have been implemented following Section II-C, calibrated to profiling data.
The draft-model compute-intensity function F^d(i, l) and verification compute-intensity function F^v(I, L) have been implemented following equations (3)-(4) with decoder-only cost scaling.

Code has been implemented for a function F_d(i, l, J_d, h1_d, h2_d) returning the draft compute intensity for one round as specified in equation (3), taking prefix length i, draft length l, and the draft model's transformer dimensions as inputs.

Code has been implemented for a function F_v(I, L, J_v, h1_v, h2_v) returning the verification compute intensity as specified in equation (4), taking batch-wise max prefix length I, batch-wise max draft length L, and the target model's transformer dimensions as inputs.

F^d and F^v scale correctly with their arguments: F^d is monotonically increasing in both i and l, and F^v is monotonically increasing in I, L, and (implicitly through model dims) larger for the verify model than the draft model at matched (i=I, l=L).
The affine per-step latency functions G_m (drafting) and G^v (verification) have been implemented following equations (5)-(6) as affine in the product b*F.
Code has been implemented for the per-token drafting latency G_m(b, F) = c_m * b * F + beta_m as specified in equation (5), parameterized by the user-side latency coefficients (c_m, beta_m).
Code has been implemented for the per-token verification latency G^v(b, F) = c_v * b * F + beta_v as specified in equation (6), parameterized by the verify-side latency coefficients (c_v, beta_v).
G_m and G^v are affine in the product b*F: doubling b*F yields a slope-consistent latency change equal to the respective c coefficient, and setting b*F=0 recovers the fixed overhead beta.
Latency coefficients are calibrated to profiling data consistent with the paper's default values.
Default user-side latency parameters (c_m, beta_m) are set to (4.0305e-11, 33.8151) in millisecond units, matching Table II.
Default verify-side latency parameters (c_v, beta_v) are set to (1.2077e-11, 95.1074) in millisecond units, matching Table II.

Code has been implemented for a profiling routine that measures drafting and verification per-step latency as a function of (batch, F) and fits the affine model in equations (5)-(6) via least squares on the collected data points.
The composed drafting and verification latencies are correctly integrated with the primitives to reproduce paper-reported timing behavior.
The per-user drafting latency computation multiplies l_m by G_m evaluated at b=1 and F=F^d(i_m, l_m) as required for local serial drafting (equation (12)).
The batch verification latency computation multiplies (L_n + 1) by G^v evaluated at b=b_n and F=F^v(I_n, L_n) as required by equation (15), where L_n and I_n are the batch-wise maxima.

Under the default single-user scenario (M=1 or N=M with b=1) with default parameters from Table II, drafting one token via G_m yields a latency dominated by beta_m near 33.82 ms, and verifying with b=1 yields a per-step latency dominated by beta_v near 95.11 ms, matching the profiled overheads.

The binary assignment constraints, batch-size definitions, batch-wise max epigraphs, drafting/verification latency, stage duration, and pipeline span constraints have been implemented as in Sections II-D and II-E.

Assignment and batch-aggregation constraints (Section II-D, Eqs. (7)-(11)) have been implemented, including binary user-to-batch assignment variables, one-batch-per-user constraint, positive-integer draft lengths, batch size definition with b_n>=1, and batch-wise max epigraph inequalities for L_n and I_n.
Code has been implemented that declares binary assignment variables x_{m,n} in {0,1} for each user m in M and each batch n in N, matching Eq. (7).
Code has been implemented enforcing the one-batch-per-user constraint sum_{n in N} x_{m,n} = 1 for every user m, matching Eq. (8).
Code has been implemented that constrains draft length l_m to positive integers with l_m in {1,...,L_ub} (Eq. (9) together with the practical upper bound L_ub used in the joint solver).
Code has been implemented defining batch size b_n = sum_{m in M} x_{m,n} with the activity constraint b_n >= 1 for every declared batch n in N (Eq. (10)).

Code has been implemented that enforces the batch-wise max epigraph inequalities L_n >= x_{m,n} * l_m and I_n >= x_{m,n} * i_m for all m,n (Eq. (11)), so that L_n and I_n act as batch-wise maxima of speculative length and prefix length.

Given a fixed assignment x with l_m specified, the implemented constraints yield L_n = max_{m: x_{m,n}=1} l_m and I_n = max_{m: x_{m,n}=1} i_m at optimality (verified on a small hand-constructed instance).

Per-user drafting latency and batch draft-completion timing (Eqs. (12)-(13)) have been implemented, coupling the local serial drafting cost with per-user communication overhead and aggregating them into batch-level draft completion times t^d_n.
Code has been implemented computing per-user drafting latency t^d_m = l_m * G_m(l_m, i_m) + tau^c_m as specified in Eq. (12), where G_m is the affine per-step drafting latency function.

Code has been implemented enforcing the batch draft-completion max epigraph t^d_n >= x_{m,n} * t^d_m for all m in M and all n in N (Eq. (13)), so t^d_n captures when all requests in batch n finish drafting and communication.

Batch verification latency and stage duration (Eqs. (14)-(15)) have been implemented, using the batch size and batch-wise maxima (L_n, I_n) via the affine verification model G^v, with stage duration constrained to cover verification.

Code has been implemented computing the batch verification latency t^v_n = G^v(b_n, F^v(L_n, I_n)) form as in Eq. (14), reflecting dependence on batch size b_n and batch-wise maxima (L_n, I_n) due to padding.

Code has been implemented enforcing the stage-duration inequality T_n >= t^v_n for every batch n in N (Eq. (15)), so that stage duration can exceed verification time to satisfy global precedence and pipeline bubbles.
Pipeline span S and precedence constraints coupling drafting, verification, and stage durations (Eqs. (16)-(19)) have been implemented, forming the steady-state cycle time over one full SD round.

Code has been implemented defining the total pipeline span S as the sum of stage durations S = sum_{n in N} T_n over all batches (Eq. (17)), representing the steady-state cycle time of one complete SD round.

Code has been implemented enforcing the pipeline precedence constraint that S covers the drafting completion time of each batch, i.e. S >= t^d_n + t^v_n (or the equivalent precedence form in Eqs. (18)-(19)) for every n in N.

Code has been implemented enforcing the pipeline precedence constraint that S covers the accumulated verification schedule up to batch n (the second precedence inequality in Eqs. (18)-(19)) for every n in N, ensuring no verification slot overlap.

Auxiliary timing variables (t^d_n, t^v_n, T_n, S) are declared as continuous non-negative variables with practical upper bounds T_ub and S_ub as described in Section III-A, matching the values (T_ub, S_ub) = (1e6, 3e6) in Table II.

On a small deterministic test instance (fixed x and l), the implemented span S equals sum_n T_n where each T_n is driven up to the tighter of (t^d_n + t^v_n) and the cumulative verification precedence bound, verifying that pipeline-bubble behavior is correctly modeled.

Practical variable bounds L_ub and I_ub are applied as upper bounds on L_n and I_n (and l_m for L_ub) with the default values (L_ub, I_ub) = (20, 1024) from Table II, tightening the MILP as described in Section III-A.
The FP16 parameter memory footprint, KV-cache size per batch, and memory feasibility constraint at the edge server have been implemented as in Section II-F.
The FP16 target-model parameter memory footprint has been implemented following the Section II-F formula for parameter memory (proportional to J^v, h_1^v, h_2^v with 2 bytes per parameter).

Code has been implemented that computes M_param for the target verification model as a function of (J^v, h_1^v, h_2^v) in FP16 (2 bytes/param), covering attention and FFN parameter counts consistent with a standard decoder-only transformer.

When evaluated on the default Qwen3-32B target model dimensions (J^v=64, h_1^v=5120, h_2^v=25600), the computed FP16 parameter memory M_param is a fixed constant independent of batching decisions and matches the analytical value produced by the Section II-F parameter-memory formula.

The per-batch KV-cache memory M_kv,n has been implemented as a function of batch size b_n, batch-wise max prefix length I_n, and batch-wise max draft length L_n, following the Section II-F KV-cache formula.

Code has been implemented that computes the KV-cache memory for batch n as a linear function of b_n * (I_n + L_n) * J^v * h_1^v in FP16 (2 bytes per KV entry for both K and V), matching the KV-cache size expression given in Section II-F.

The KV-cache computation correctly uses the batch-wise maxima L_n and I_n (as defined by the epigraph constraints in Section II-D) rather than per-user l_m and i_m, so padding to the batch max is accounted for.
The memory feasibility constraint M_param + M_kv,n <= Gamma^v_max has been implemented and enforced as a hard constraint in the x-subproblem MILP for every batch n.

Code has been implemented that, for each batch n, adds a linear (in b_n, L_n, I_n) memory constraint M_param + M_kv,n <= Gamma^v_max to the optimization model, using the default Gamma^v_max = 8.0e10 bytes from Table II.

Given a candidate batching assignment that would exceed Gamma^v_max (e.g., packing all M=6 users into one batch with default i_m=512 and l_m up to L_ub=20), the solver rejects it as infeasible while accepting an assignment whose computed M_param + M_kv,n stays below Gamma^v_max.

The memory constraint is applied to all N batches simultaneously (one constraint per stage n in {1,...,N}) rather than only to a single aggregate batch, matching the per-batch formulation in Section II-F.
The throughput objective R = U(l)/S and the joint optimization problem over (x, l, N, auxiliary variables) have been formulated correctly per Section II-G.
The throughput expression R = U(l)/S has been implemented as a function combining the utility U(l) and the pipeline span S.
Code has been implemented that computes throughput R as U(l) divided by S, taking U(l) from the utility model of Section II-B and S from the pipeline span expression in Equation (17).
Code has been implemented that reports throughput in token/s by multiplying R (in token/ms) by 1000, consistent with the units described in Section IV-A.
The joint optimization problem (Equation 22) has been formulated with the correct decision variables and objective.

The optimization problem declares the decision variables to include the batch count N, the user-to-batch assignment matrix x, the per-user integer draft lengths l, and the auxiliary timing/batch variables (b_n, L_n, I_n, t_n^d, t_n^v, T_n, S).
The formulation sets the objective to maximize R = U(l)/S (equivalently maximize throughput) rather than minimize latency or any other proxy.
The batch count N is constrained to the integer range {2, ..., M} as specified in Section II-A and Equation (22).

The joint problem aggregates all constraint families from Sections II-D, II-E, and II-F (assignment, batch-aggregation, latency-coupling, pipeline precedence, and memory feasibility) into a single feasible set applied to the throughput-maximization objective.
The formulation supports the stationary-workload interpretation used to justify single-round throughput evaluation.

Code has been implemented that evaluates throughput over a single representative SD round (one pipeline cycle), treating im and other per-user parameters as constants within the optimization horizon, consistent with Section II-A and II-G.
The x-subproblem MILP for batch assignment and batch-wise timing variables under fixed l has been implemented (Section III-B) using SCIP/PySCIPOpt.
The MILP model construction for the x-subproblem is in place.

Code has been implemented that instantiates a PySCIPOpt Model for the x-subproblem given fixed integer draft lengths l and current problem parameters (M, N, alphas, prefix lengths, latency/memory coefficients, bounds).
Code has been implemented that declares binary assignment variables x_{m,n} for m in {1,...,M} and n in {1,...,N} and adds the one-batch-per-user constraint sum_n x_{m,n} = 1 for each user m.
Code has been implemented that defines the batch-size variable b_n = sum_m x_{m,n} for each batch n and enforces b_n >= 1 to guarantee every declared batch is active.
Code has been implemented that adds batch-wise max epigraph constraints L_n >= x_{m,n} * l_m and I_n >= x_{m,n} * i_m for all m, n, using the fixed l values so these remain linear.

Code has been implemented that encodes per-user drafting completion via t^d_n >= x_{m,n} * (l_m * G_m(i_m + L_n, ...) + tau^c_m)-style epigraph constraints so t^d_n captures the batch-n drafting-plus-communication completion time.
Code has been implemented that adds the batch verification latency definition t^v_n = G^v(b_n, L_n, I_n) and the stage-duration constraints T_n >= t^v_n, T_n >= t^d_n enforcing pipeline precedence.

Code has been implemented that adds the pipeline-span variable S with S = sum_n T_n and the memory feasibility constraint Mem_params + sum-of-KV-cache(b_n, I_n + L_n) <= Gamma^v_max at the edge server.
Code has been implemented that imposes the practical upper bounds (L_ub, I_ub, T_ub, S_ub) on the corresponding variables to tighten the MILP as described in Section III-A.
The x-subproblem objective and solve routine behave correctly.
Code has been implemented that sets the x-subproblem objective to minimize S (equivalently maximize R = U(l)/S since U(l) is constant for fixed l), and calls model.optimize() through PySCIPOpt.

Code has been implemented that, after solving, extracts the assignment matrix x (rounded from binary variables) along with b_n, L_n, I_n, t^d_n, t^v_n, T_n, and S, and returns them for use by the alternating outer loop.

For a small deterministic instance (e.g., M=4, N=2, homogeneous parameters), the solved x-subproblem returns a feasible assignment satisfying sum_n x_{m,n}=1, b_n>=1, memory constraint, and yields the batch-balanced grouping expected under homogeneity.

depends_on: Throughput Objective and Joint Optimization Formulation

sub_tasks.requirements: The l-subproblem using binary selectors for integer draft length, lookup utility, and Dinkelbach's method for fractional objective handling has been implemented as in Section III-C.
Binary selector reformulation of integer draft length lm has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that introduces binary selector variables y_{m,k} for k in {1,...,L_ub} for each user m, with constraint sum_k y_{m,k} = 1 enforcing exactly one selected draft length per user.
Code has been implemented that reconstructs lm as lm = sum_k k * y_{m,k} using the binary selectors, so that lm is an integer in {1,...,L_ub}.
Code has been implemented that enforces the upper bound lm <= L_ub via the binary selector domain, using the L_ub value (=20) from Table II.
Lookup utility formulation and batch-wise max-consistency for L_n have been implemented.

Code has been implemented that precomputes the lookup utility values u_m(k) = (1 - alpha_m^k)/(1 - alpha_m) + 1 for each user m and each candidate draft length k in {1,...,L_ub}, so that u_m(lm) becomes the linear expression sum_k u_m(k) * y_{m,k}.
Code has been implemented that enforces max-consistency L_n >= lm for all users m in B_n(x) (the fixed user set of batch n given x), using the batch assignment from the x-subproblem.
Dinkelbach's parametric method for the fractional throughput objective has been implemented per Eqs. (34)-(36).
Code has been implemented that maintains a Dinkelbach parameter r (throughput estimate) initialized to r=0 (or a small positive value) at the start of each l-subproblem.

Code has been implemented that at each Dinkelbach iteration t solves the inner MILP maximizing U(l) - r^(t) * S subject to all l-related constraints (binary selectors, L_n consistency, latency/timing constraints with x fixed, memory constraint, variable bounds).
Code has been implemented that updates r^(t+1) = U(l^(t+1)) / S^(t+1) using the optimal l and S from the current inner MILP solution, per Eq. (35).
Code has been implemented that terminates the Dinkelbach loop when |U(l^(t+1)) - r^(t) * S^(t+1)| falls below a tolerance (or an equivalent throughput-change threshold is met), per Eq. (36).
Inner MILP formulation and solver integration for the l-subproblem have been implemented.

Code has been implemented that assembles the inner MILP with objective sum_m sum_k u_m(k) * y_{m,k} - r * S and includes all latency-coupling constraints (drafting latency t^d_m = lm * G_m, batch draft-time epigraph t^d_n >= t^d_m + tau^c_m, verification latency t^v_n = G^v, stage duration T_n >= t^v_n, pipeline span S = sum_n T_n, precedence S >= t^d_n + t^v_n) with x fixed.

Code has been implemented that enforces the practical variable bounds (L_ub=20, I_ub=1024, T_ub=1e6, S_ub=3e6) as upper bounds on the corresponding MILP variables to tighten and stabilize the l-subproblem.
Code has been implemented that solves the inner MILP by invoking SCIP through the PySCIPOpt Python interface.

Code has been implemented that includes the FP16 memory feasibility constraint (parameter footprint + KV-cache <= Gamma^v_max = 8.0e10) inside the l-subproblem MILP so that draft-length choices respect edge-server memory limits.
Behavioral correctness of the l-subproblem solver has been verified.
On a small fixed-x instance, the l-subproblem returns integer draft lengths lm in {1,...,L_ub} for every user, and the reconstructed lm equals the argmax_k y_{m,k} from the binary selectors.

The Dinkelbach iteration produces a monotonically non-decreasing throughput estimate r across successive iterations on a representative instance, and converges within a bounded number of iterations (e.g., <= 20) under the specified tolerance.
At Dinkelbach convergence, the returned solution satisfies U(l*)/S* = r* within the specified tolerance, confirming correct fractional-to-parametric reduction.

depends_on: Throughput Objective and Joint Optimization Formulation

sub_tasks.requirements: The full DiP-SD algorithm (Algorithm 1) — outer scan over N, alternating x/l updates, convergence checking, and best-N selection — has been implemented.
The top-level DiP-SD solver entry point exists and exposes the algorithmic interface described in Algorithm 1.

Code has been implemented that provides a callable DiP-SD solver function/class taking inputs (M, system parameters, L_ub, tolerances, solver limits) and returning (N*, x*, l*, R*) as specified in Algorithm 1's Require/Ensure clauses.
Code has been implemented that accepts and applies the practical variable bounds (L_ub, I_ub, T_ub, S_ub) to tighten the MILPs, plumbing them through to both subproblems.
The outer batch-count scan loop over N in {2, ..., M} has been implemented.
Code has been implemented that iterates N from 2 to M inclusive, invoking the alternating optimization for each N and storing the converged throughput R*(N) per line 8 of Algorithm 1.

The scan behaves such that when a candidate N yields an infeasible subproblem (e.g., memory constraint violated), it is skipped or recorded with -infinity throughput without aborting the overall scan.
The inner alternating optimization between the x-subproblem and the l-subproblem has been implemented per Algorithm 1 lines 2-7.
Code has been implemented that initializes l^(0) (e.g., using the default initial draft length l_m = 7) and iteration counter r = 0 before entering the alternating loop.

In each alternating iteration, the x-subproblem is solved first with fixed l^(r) to yield x^(r+1), and then the l-subproblem is solved with fixed x^(r+1) to yield l^(r+1), matching the update ordering of Algorithm 1 lines 4-5.
Code has been implemented that computes the throughput R(N) = U(l)/S from the current (x, l) iterate at the end of each alternating iteration for use in convergence checking.
The convergence criterion for the outer alternating loop has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that terminates the alternating loop when l is unchanged between successive iterations AND the absolute (or relative) throughput change falls below the configured tolerance, per Section III-A.
The alternating loop enforces a maximum-iteration safeguard so it terminates even if the tolerance condition is not met, avoiding infinite loops.
The best-N selection step and final solution assembly have been implemented.
Code has been implemented that computes N* = argmax_{N in {2,...,M}} R*(N) and returns the associated (x*, l*, R*) as the final DiP-SD solution, per Algorithm 1 line 9 and equation in Section III-D.

When invoked on a homogeneous default configuration (M=6, alpha_m=0.78, defaults from Table II), the solver returns a self-consistent tuple where R* equals U(l*)/S evaluated at the returned (x*, l*), with S computed via the pipeline-span definition (17).
End-to-end DiP-SD throughput on the default homogeneous configuration matches the paper's reported value.

Running DiP-SD end-to-end on M=6, alpha_m=0.78, and all other Table II defaults produces a throughput consistent with the paper's approximate 1.38x speedup over AD w/ greedy batching at the default acceptance rate (Section IV-B1).

depends_on: Joint Solver: l-Subproblem with Binary Reformulation and Dinkelbach

sub_tasks.requirements: The four baseline methods — AD, AD w/ greedy batching, DiP-SD w/o batching, and DiP-SD w/ fixed l_m=7 — have been implemented as described in Section IV-A.
The AD (autoregressive decoding) baseline has been implemented as edge-only target-model decoding without speculative drafting and without batching.
Code has been implemented that computes AD per-round latency using the verification latency model G^v with batch size b=1 (single user, no batching) and no drafting/communication contribution.

Code has been implemented so that AD throughput is computed as one accepted token per verification step divided by verification latency (l_m implicitly 0, U=1 per user per round) and is independent of user number M.
AD throughput remains constant across all sweeps over M in {2,...,14} and over alpha_m in {0.70,...,0.95}, matching the flat AD curves in Fig. 3(a) and Fig. 3(b).

The AD w/ greedy batching baseline has been implemented as AD with a memory-feasible greedy batching heuristic that sorts users by i_m in descending order and packs them sequentially into batches until the memory bound would be violated.
Code has been implemented that sorts the user set by prefix length i_m in descending order prior to batch packing.

Code has been implemented that packs sorted users sequentially into the current batch and opens a new batch when adding the next user would violate the memory constraint gamma^v_max (Eq. 21), using the KV-cache expression with the batch-wise max prefix length.

Code has been implemented that, given the greedy batching assignment, computes the pipeline span S as the sum of verification latencies over batches (no drafting since AD) and reports throughput R = M / S (one accepted token per user per round).
AD w/ greedy batching throughput grows approximately linearly with M in the homogeneous sweep M in {2,4,...,14}, matching the linear trend shown in Fig. 3(a).
The DiP-SD w/o batching baseline has been implemented by forcing N=M with one user per batch and optimizing only the draft-length vector l.
Code has been implemented that fixes N=M and constructs the assignment x as the identity mapping (user m assigned uniquely to batch m, batch size b_n=1 for all n), bypassing the x-subproblem.
Code has been implemented that invokes the l-subproblem solver (binary reformulation + Dinkelbach) with the fixed one-per-batch assignment to obtain optimal integer draft lengths l_m in {1,...,L_ub}.
DiP-SD w/o batching throughput first increases with M and then plateaus in the homogeneous M sweep, matching the trend in Fig. 3(a).
